body:
Why Gujarat has several environmental authorities

Gujarat has major industrial centres, ports, agricultural regions, cities, forests, wetlands and coastal ecosystems. Development in these areas can affect air, water, land, biodiversity and public health. Environmental regulation therefore involves several institutions, each responsible for a different aspect of protection.

Environmental permission is not a single licence. A project may need permission under pollution-control laws, environmental impact assessment rules, coastal regulations, forest laws or wildlife laws. Local land-use and building permissions may also apply. The requirements depend on the type, size, location and likely effects of the activity.

Environmental clearance: Prior approval required for specified projects or activities under the Environmental Impact Assessment Notification, 2006, as amended. It examines their likely environmental impacts and proposed safeguards.

Pollution-control consent: Permission under the applicable water and air pollution laws to establish or operate an activity, subject to conditions. Certain categories are exempt from separate consent requirements.

The principal institutions

InstitutionMain responsibilityTypical matter
Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB)Prevention and control of pollutionIndustrial emissions, wastewater, consent and specified waste authorisations
State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA), GujaratDecision on applicable Category B environmental-clearance proposalsPrior environmental clearance based on expert appraisal
Gujarat Coastal Zone Management Authority (GCZMA)Coastal Regulation Zone compliance and scrutinyDevelopment proposed in regulated coastal areas
State Forest Department and wildlife authoritiesForest and wildlife conservationForest-land diversion and activities affecting protected areas
Gujarat Biodiversity Board and local Biodiversity Management CommitteesConservation and sustainable use of biological resourcesLocal biodiversity records and access-related regulation
Municipal and rural local bodiesLocal sanitation, waste services and civic infrastructureSolid waste, drainage, public sanitation and local permissions

National laws and state implementation

Parliament has enacted major environmental laws that operate across India. Important examples are the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The last is an umbrella law under which important notifications and waste-management rules have been issued.

The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) administers important central environmental functions. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) coordinates pollution-control activities nationally, while GPCB implements pollution-control responsibilities within Gujarat. Other state-level authorities perform separate functions under the relevant laws.

Why permissions can overlap

Consider a proposed industrial unit near Gujarat's coast. Its manufacturing process may require GPCB oversight. Its size or activity may bring it under the Environmental Impact Assessment Notification. Its location may require Coastal Regulation Zone scrutiny. If forest land or a protected wildlife area is affected, further statutory requirements arise. These are different legal questions, even when they concern the same project.

Industrial estates do not eliminate environmental duties

The Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) develops industrial estates and provides infrastructure such as roads, water supply and, in some estates, common treatment facilities. It is an industrial-development institution, not a substitute for GPCB, SEIAA or GCZMA. An allotted industrial plot or an estate-level approval does not automatically satisfy every legal obligation of an individual unit.

Prelims focus

  • Water pollution: Water Act, 1974.
  • Air pollution: Air Act, 1981.
  • Environmental umbrella legislation: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
  • GPCB regulates pollution; SEIAA decides applicable state-level environmental-clearance proposals.
  • GCZMA deals with Coastal Regulation Zone matters.
  • Trap: GIDC allotment is not equivalent to all environmental approvals.

[Sources: Government of India, Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; MoEFCC, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, paragraphs 2–4; GIDC, official website, Infrastructure Development and Plug and Play sections. Official online sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Gujarat's Environmental Governance: Institutions and Their Responsibilities

body:
Establishment and purpose

The Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) is Gujarat's principal state-level pollution-control regulator. The Government of Gujarat constituted it on 15 October 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. Its responsibilities subsequently expanded to include functions under the Air Act and environmental rules entrusted to state pollution control boards.

GPCB seeks to prevent, control and reduce pollution. Its work covers both industrial activities and environmental conditions outside factory premises. Pollution may travel through rivers, groundwater, air or soil, so regulation cannot be confined to the factory boundary.

The main statutory foundations

LawYearPrincipal relevance
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act1974Prevention and control of water pollution; consent relating to sewage and trade-effluent discharges
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act1981Prevention and control of air pollution; consent for covered industrial plants in air pollution control areas
Environment (Protection) Act1986Central framework for environmental standards, directions and rules, including specified waste-management requirements

Section 25 of the Water Act is a principal provision governing prior consent for covered new outlets, discharges and establishments. Section 21 of the Air Act governs consent concerning covered industrial plants in air pollution control areas. These requirements must be read with the exemptions notified in 2024 and the applicable consent rules.

What GPCB does

Granting and regulating consent

For activities that require pollution-control consent, GPCB examines the proposed process, likely wastewater and air emissions, pollution-control equipment and compliance arrangements. A consent may specify discharge standards, emission limits, treatment requirements, monitoring obligations and conditions for operation.

Environmental monitoring

GPCB monitors ambient air and water quality and assesses pollution from regulated activities. Its programmes include monitoring of important Gujarat rivers such as the Narmada, Tapi, Mahi and Sabarmati. Monitoring environmental quality differs from granting an individual industry's consent: the former assesses environmental conditions, while the latter regulates a specified activity.

Inspection and enforcement

Under the relevant laws, authorised officers may inspect facilities, examine records and take samples. Where violations are established, statutory directions and other enforcement measures may follow. Consent does not give an operator permission to exceed the limits written into it.

Specified waste authorisations

GPCB also performs responsibilities under rules such as the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, as amended. A facility handling covered hazardous waste may need the appropriate authorisation and must follow conditions for storage, transport, treatment and disposal.

CPCB and GPCB are not interchangeable

The CPCB is established at the national level under the Water Act. It coordinates programmes, provides technical guidance and undertakes functions assigned under central environmental laws. GPCB is the corresponding board responsible for important pollution-control functions in Gujarat. National standards and directions may therefore be implemented through state-level consent, inspection and enforcement.

A textile-processing unit

A textile-processing unit may generate wastewater containing dyes or other chemicals. GPCB's concern is whether the unit has applicable consent and whether its treatment and discharge comply with the prescribed conditions. The fact that the unit employs many people or is located in an industrial estate does not remove these pollution-control obligations.

What GPCB does not normally decide

GPCB is not the general authority that grants prior environmental clearance under the EIA Notification, nor does it replace forest-diversion approval or Coastal Regulation Zone permission. It can nevertheless participate in those processes by supplying pollution-related observations or conducting the prescribed public hearing.

Prelims focus

  • GPCB was constituted on 15 October 1974 under the Water Act, 1974.
  • Water Act, Section 25: a principal statutory consent provision.
  • Air Act, Section 21: consent for covered industrial plants.
  • CPCB is the central board; GPCB is the state board for Gujarat.
  • GPCB monitors pollution, regulates applicable consents and exercises enforcement powers.
  • Trap: Pollution-control consent and prior environmental clearance are different legal instruments.

[Sources: GPCB, About Us, official PM GatiShakti government portal, consulted 1 November 2026; Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, Sections 16, 17 and 25; Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, Section 21; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, sections on air and water pollution.]

pictures.alt: CPCB coordinates nationally; GPCB regulates Gujarat industries through covered water and air consents, then continues monitoring, inspection and enforcement.
pictures.caption: National coordination and state-level pollution regulation.

title: Gujarat Pollution Control Board: Functions and Legal Powers

body:
Why industrial consent has different stages

An industry may create pollution during construction, installation, trial production or regular operation. Pollution-control legislation therefore provides consent mechanisms connected with establishing and operating covered activities. The exact requirements depend on the industry's classification and the law applicable on the relevant date.

Consent to Establish

Consent to Establish (CTE) is the pollution-control consent ordinarily associated with setting up a covered industrial activity before establishment, where a separate CTE remains legally required. At this stage, the regulator can examine site suitability and proposed arrangements for controlling pollution.

Consent to Operate

Consent to Operate (CTO) is the applicable pollution-control consent for commencing and continuing regulated operations. It concerns the actual ability of the unit to comply with discharge, emission and other conditions. Under the 2026 consent guidelines, CTO, once granted, remains valid until cancelled; the unit must comply with its consent conditions and obtain amendments when required.

CTE concerns the establishment stage; CTO concerns the operating stage. However, not every unit must obtain both: the legal exemptions described below are important.

Consolidated Consent and Authorisation

GPCB uses the term Consolidated Consent and Authorisation (CCA) for an administrative instrument that consolidates applicable pollution-control consents and specified authorisations. This can bring requirements under different laws into one document. It does not turn CCA into an environmental clearance under the EIA Notification or into a forest or coastal permission.

GPCB has also used the XGN (Xtended Green Node) electronic system for regulatory applications and administration. Online filing changes how an application is processed; it does not change which legal authority has power to decide it.

Important consent exemptions introduced in 2024

Two central notifications dated 12 November 2024, G.S.R. 702(E) under the Air Act and G.S.R. 703(E) under the Water Act, changed the usual consent position:

  • Projects requiring and obtaining prior environmental clearance: A separate CTE under the Water and Air Acts is not required under the notified exemption. Pollution-control safeguards are considered during environmental clearance, with the state pollution control board consulted. The relevant fees and integrated safeguards remain applicable. CTO continues to apply where the activity otherwise requires it.
  • White-category activities: Activities covered by the non-polluting White category are exempt from both CTE and CTO under the notified framework. They must intimate GPCB about their operations through a self-declaration of compliance with applicable environmental laws and remain subject to other applicable environmental laws.

The Ministry issued implementation procedures in November 2024, with a modification in January 2025. GPCB adopted the White-category exemption through its 5 June 2025 office order. The exemption removes specified consents; it does not authorise pollution or override forest, coastal, land-use or other legal restrictions.

Classification of industries

Pollution-control boards use industrial categories to reflect pollution potential and regulatory requirements. The revised CPCB classification adopted by GPCB identifies Red, Orange, Green, White and Blue categories. Red generally indicates greater pollution potential than Orange or Green. White identifies listed activities with negligible pollution potential that qualify for the notified consent exemption. Blue is a distinct category associated with specified environmental-management or essential environmental-service activities; it should not simply be treated as another step in an increasing pollution ranking.

An industry's classification depends on its actual activity and the current official list, not merely its business name or the fact that it is a small enterprise.

Compliance after permission

Depending on the activity and consent conditions, a unit may have to operate an effluent treatment plant (ETP), control air emissions, maintain records, submit monitoring results, manage hazardous waste safely and prevent unauthorised discharges. Several industries may use a common effluent treatment plant (CETP), but membership of a CETP does not automatically excuse an individual unit from meeting its own inlet standards and consent conditions.

Industries operating in clusters such as Vapi, Ankleshwar and Dahej illustrate why pollution management may require both individual-unit controls and common environmental infrastructure.

Prelims focus

  • CTE: establishment-stage consent, where separately required.
  • CTO: operation-stage consent, where required.
  • CCA: Consolidated Consent and Authorisation.
  • G.S.R. 702(E) and 703(E), dated 12 November 2024, provide important consent exemptions.
  • GPCB's White-category exemption order is dated 5 June 2025.
  • Trap: An EC-holding project may be exempt from separate CTE but still require CTO.

[Sources: MoEFCC, G.S.R. 702(E) and G.S.R. 703(E), 12 November 2024; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Lok Sabha reply on Changes in Environmental Clearances Policy, 3 February 2025; GPCB, Office Order dated 5 June 2025 concerning White-category consent exemption, reproduced in the GPCB material filed before the National Green Tribunal in Original Application 109 of 2025; GIDC, Plug and Play and Industrial Infrastructure sections. Official sources consulted 1 November 2026.]
